title: Expectations vs. Realities: The Cost of MSE-Optimal Forecasting Under Conditional Uncertainty

problem.claim: Point-wise MSE evaluation can treat the conditional mean as sufficient even when it is unrepresentative of typical realized values at longer forecasting horizons.

gap.claim: MSE-only evaluation does not account for the trade-off between point accuracy and the marginal realism of realized futures under conditional uncertainty.

contributions.claim: The paper formalizes a conditional uncertainty gap and proves that a nonzero gap prevents any deterministic predictor from simultaneously minimizing MSE and matching the marginal distribution of realized futures.
The paper characterizes the accuracy–realism frontier using controlled stochastic dynamical systems and nine real-world forecasting benchmarks.

The paper shows that forecasting strategies occupy different regions of the accuracy–realism frontier, with direct multi-output predictors nearer the accuracy-optimal extreme and recursive or sample-based strategies favoring marginal realism.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across nine real-world forecasting benchmarks, relaxations in MSE of at most 5% frequently produced median marginal-realism improvements of 17.3%, with gains exceeding 30% on some datasets.

Increasing conditional uncertainty with forecast horizon was associated with a pronounced Pareto front separating under-dispersed MSE-optimal predictors from methods with more realistic marginal variability.

narrative_sequence.summary: MSF is commonly evaluated with point-wise MSE, implicitly treating the conditional mean as sufficient.
Under conditional uncertainty, the conditional expectation can become unrepresentative of typical realized values at longer horizons.
A conditional uncertainty gap formalizes the incompatibility between deterministic MSE minimization and matching the marginal distribution of realized futures.
Controlled systems and nine benchmarks reveal an accuracy–realism frontier, including disproportionate realism gains from small MSE relaxations.
Forecasting strategy and inference selection are framed as navigation of an unavoidable accuracy–realism trade-off.

source_observation.claim: Small MSE relaxations frequently yielded much larger gains in marginal realism.

interpretation.claim: Strict optimization of a point-error metric can impose a substantial realism cost under conditional uncertainty.

application.claim: Forecasting evaluation and model selection should inspect accuracy–realism trade-offs rather than relying exclusively on MSE.

exception.claim: The reported gains may depend on forecast horizon, conditional uncertainty, datasets, and the specific realism metric or evaluation setup.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the conditional uncertainty gap's formal definition.
The abstract does not identify the nine real-world benchmarks or the marginal-realism metric.
The abstract does not provide statistical uncertainty, baselines, or experimental implementation details.
